Title: Role of environmental disclosure policy on access to finance: evidence from crowdfunding
Authors: John Jianqiu Bai, Yi Cao, Xiumin Martin, Chi Wan
Abstract: Abstract We study the impact of an online market’s policy (environmental policy) offering entrepreneurs the option to disclose their environmental engagement on entrepreneurship outcomes, using Kickstarter as a laboratory. Following the policy’s implementation, 32.4% of entrepreneurs opted to disclose their environmental commitments. Using the passage of the environmental policy as an instrument, we show that environmental commitment improves funding outcomes, with the funding success rate increasing by 13.2% and the pledged funding ratio by 8.7%. Environmental commitment also attracts more environmentally conscious backers and brings in new backers, which likely contributes to these improved outcomes. However, environmental commitment does not have a material impact on the ultimate project success rate and significantly delays project delivery. Overall, the evidence suggests that Kickstarter’s nudge policy encourages entrepreneurs’ environmental engagement and helps them expand access to environmentally conscious backers by internalizing backers’ environmental preferences.

Title: The Link Between Explicit AI-Generated Images and Offline Crime
Authors: Siddharth Bhattacharya, Yun Young Hur, Gal Oestreicher-Singer
Abstract: A new research study reveals that broad availability of AI-generated adult content may have led to sharp increases in sexual criminality. An analysis of detailed crime data released by Japan’s National Police Agency found that in periods of peak engagement with material tagged as AI-generated and adults-only, there were statistically significant increases in rape. This may point to looming reputational and legal risk for companies providing tools and venues for such content.

Title: Inflation and Corporate Credit Risk: Global Evidence
Authors: Buhui Qiu, Thomas To, Gaiyan Zhang
Affiliations: University of Sydney Business School, The University of Sydney; Ed G. Smith College of Business, University of Missouri-St. Louis
Abstract: Abstract We provide novel international evidence that inflation is positively associated with corporate credit risk on average. A 1-standard-deviation increase in inflation is associated with a 21-basis-point increase in next-year credit default swap spreads. Importantly, this relationship is convex: it is negative or weak at low inflation levels but much more positive in high-inflation environments. The positive relation between inflation and credit risk is stronger for firms with greater refinancing vulnerability and more rigid operating cash flows, and in countries with more inflation-responsive monetary regimes and weaker institutional environments. Our findings are consistent with opposing roles for debt rigidity and operating rigidity.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Macroeconomic Fundamentals and the Shape of Sovereign Credit Risk
Authors: Daniele Bianchi, Teng Jiao
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Reinforcement learning for joint scheduling in robotic mobile fulfillment systems
Authors: Yunyang Lu, Lindong Liu, Yan Zhu, Chengcheng Yu
Abstract: Robotic mobile fulfillment systems (RMFSs) are revolutionizing e-Commerce by automating the transport of product pods to workstations, reducing labor costs, and improving order fulfillment efficiency. However, this automation introduces new operational complexities that require innovative solutions. In this paper, we tackle the primary scheduling issues that arise during the order processing phase, including pod retrieval, pod repositioning, and robot assignment. We utilize the Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework as our decision-making model to minimize the system's makespan. To solve the problem, we propose a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based method for the RMFS joint scheduling problem, and introduce several effective rules to constrain the search space, significantly accelerating the training process. We evaluate the performance of our algorithms on both small scenarios based on synthetic data and large-scale scenarios based on real-world data. The computational results demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms for daily use. In particular, joint optimization substantially outperforms decoupled optimization, highlighting the necessity of optimizing in an integrated manner. Through the analysis of the value function and numerical studies, we identify three key drivers of the makespan: task efficiency, visit frequency, and robot coordination. Reducing the makespan requires improving these three factors jointly. Our numerical study shows that adding more robots beyond a certain threshold yields diminishing returns, and robot coordination is more critical than individual efficiency during peak demand periods. Additionally, warehouses with a concentrated or a dispersed storage strategy perform better than those with a moderate storage strategy.

Title: A novel meta-frontier super-efficiency data envelopment analysis approach capable of unbiased identification of technology gaps
Authors: Dawei Wang, Feng Yang, Lili Liu, Sheng Ang

Title: Capital Services in Global Value Chains
Authors: Xiang Ding
Affiliations: Georgetown University
Abstract: Abstract This article constructs the first global data set on intersectoral capital service expenditures. I use these data to disaggregate capital services and intermediate inputs in a dynamic multisector trade model. Steady-state allocations and responses to shocks are determined by a capital-augmented global input-output matrix. Two properties of the measured network deliver larger long-run consumption gains from globalization than existing estimates, as well as larger gains in more capital-intensive countries. First, more trade-exposed sectors supply capital to more consumption-influential producers. Second, heterogeneity in the network reallocates sectoral expenditures toward producers with larger declines in capital rental prices. These reallocations raise capital incomes and lower consumption price indices.

Title: Macro Shocks and Firm Dynamics with Oligopolistic Financial Intermediaries
Authors: Alessandro T Villa
Affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
Abstract: Abstract Motivated by a secular increase in the concentration of the U.S. banking industry, I develop a new macroeconomic model with oligopolistic financial intermediaries and heterogeneous firms. Market power allows banks to price discriminate and charge firm-specific markups, exerting greater market power over productive and more financially constrained firms. This dampens capital accumulation and amplifies the effects of macroeconomic shocks. During a crisis, banks exploit the higher share of financially constrained firms to extract higher markups, inducing a larger decline in real activity. When a large bank fails, the remaining banks use their increased market power to restrict credit supply, worsening and prolonging the downturn.

Title: Is home bias biased? New evidence from the investment fund sector
Authors: Claudia Lambert, Luis Molestina Vivar, Michael Wedow
Affiliations: Directorate General Macroprudential Policy and Financial Stability, European Central Bank , Frankfurt 60314; Directorate General Monetary Policy, European Central Bank , Frankfurt 60314
Abstract: Abstract Investment funds hold disproportionately more domestic than foreign stocks, which has been attributed to stock market development and familiarity factors such as language and distance. However, the literature typically assumes that funds represent investors in their country of incorporation, neglecting the substantial allocation of investors’ assets to foreign funds domiciled in financial centers. Using a novel “look-through approach” that combines supervisory holdings statistics with granular security-level fund portfolios, we provide a more accurate view of investors’ indirect equity allocations, independent of the fund’s legal country of incorporation. Our findings reveal three key insights. First, home bias estimates are significantly smaller than previously documented, reflecting greater geographical portfolio diversification through investment funds. Second, in most euro area countries, home bias is primarily driven by country-specific rather than common-currency preferences. Third, familiarity plays a larger role in cross-border investments for households than for institutional fund investors, highlighting the importance of investor sophistication.

Title: “Megadeal” Subsidies, Local Spillovers, and Corporate Innovation
Authors: Yoojin Lee, Shaphan Ng, Aruhn Venkat
Affiliations: College of Business California State University Long Beach; School of Accountancy Singapore Management University; School of Business University of California Riverside
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether the largest place‐based, firm‐specific corporate subsidies (“Megadeals”) awarded by state and local governments affect local firms’ innovation. First, we document that (1) subsidy firms innovate in the subsidized county and (2) subsidy firms bring inventors from other counties into the subsidized county, consistent with subsidy firms generating new knowledge locally. In our main test, we use a stacked cohort design with stringent fixed effects to document that local firms increase patenting following a Megadeal. Cross‐sectionally, effects are increasing (1) in subsidy firm innovativeness, (2) in the technological closeness of subsidy firms and local firms, (3) when subsidy and local firms share an industry, and (4) when the subsidized location has a heavy college presence. Additionally, we document that following a Megadeal, local firms increasingly make citations to subsidy firm patents and that the patent similarity of local and subsidy firms increases. We document that subsidy firm inventors are more likely to move to local firms following a Megadeal. We also find that subsidies for labs, headquarters, and high‐tech manufacturing plants drive our main results. These results are consistent with knowledge spillovers being one channel through which we observe an increase in local firm patenting following Megadeals.

Title: Guanxi Institution and Entrepreneurship in China: A Societal-Level Analysis With Evidence From Regional Panel Data (1998–2010)
Authors: Wubiao Zhou, Susan Schwarz
Affiliations: University of Birmingham, UK; King’s College London, UK
Abstract: Despite extensive existing research at the individual/organizational level, it is unclear whether guanxi – predominantly conceptualized at the micro level – supports or constrains entrepreneurship at the societal level. Drawing on institutional theory and the recent guanxi literature conceptualizing guanxi as an informal institution, this study examines the effect of guanxi on entrepreneurship at the societal level by arguing that guanxi as an informal institution can both substitute for and compete with formal institutions. Specifically, we argue that guanxi institution facilitates societal-level entrepreneurship up to a point due to its stronger substitution effect for formal institutions than the competing effect. However, beyond that threshold point, guanxi reduces entrepreneurship stocks because the competing effect with formal institutions is stronger than the substitution effect. We also argue that development of formal institutions can attenuate the main inverted-U-shaped effect of guanxi institution on societal-level entrepreneurship. Fixed effects results with provincial-level panel data from China provide strong support for the hypotheses. This study contributes to the literatures on guanxi and on the role of informal institutions in entrepreneurship.

Title: Ripples of Emotion: Unraveling the Dynamics of Emotion Flows and User Engagement in Online Healthcare Communities
Authors: Tongxin Zhou, Jingyi Sun
Affiliations: Department of Information Systems, W. P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona 85287; Information Systems and Analytics Area, School of Business, Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, New Jersey 07030
Abstract: Online healthcare communities are an important source of peer support for individuals managing chronic illnesses, mental health challenges, and stigmatized health conditions. Emotional interactions are central to this support, and yet their effects may extend well beyond the original conversation. Our study examines how emotional experiences accumulate over time by analyzing 65,740 reply interactions in an online HIV community. We find that emotional exchanges generate lasting ripple effects across the community. Users who receive more positive sentiment are more likely to remain active in writing replies and express positive sentiment in later interactions, whereas receiving more negative sentiment is associated with lower participation and less positive expression. We also find that users’ own emotional expressions shape how others subsequently respond to them: Positive expressions are associated with more replies and more positive responses, whereas negative expressions are associated with fewer and less positive responses. These effects extend across users, threads, topics, and local social clusters and are especially strong for feeling-oriented messages. The findings suggest that community managers should monitor emotional patterns at the community level, not only within individual conversations, and consider interventions that encourage constructive emotional exchanges while preventing negative emotional dynamics from becoming self-reinforcing.

Title: The Indirect Disclosure Effect: How Disclosing Generative AI Use Impacts Human Creative Collaboration with AI
Authors: Ekaterina Jussupow, Kevin Bauer, Rebecca Maria Heigl, Benjamin Vogt, Oliver Hinz
Affiliations: Technical University of Darmstadt, 64289 Darmstadt, Germany; Goethe University Frankfurt, 60323 Frankfurt am Main, Germany; Zhejiang Wanli University, Ningbo 315100, China
Abstract: Generative AI disclosure rules aim to protect audiences from deception, preserving human creativity and self-expression. Yet disclosure may change not only how audiences evaluate creative work but also how creators produce it. In two experiments involving collaboration with a text-to-image generative AI tool, we identify an indirect disclosure effect. When creators anticipated that their AI use would be disclosed to a lay audience, most withdrew from the creative process and gave the AI greater control. They did so because they feared that audiences would discount their human creative agency and fail to recognize the work as an expression of their creative selves. The resulting images reflected more computational than human creativity: audiences viewed them as more novel but less appealing and lower in quality. This withdrawal did not occur when creators expected evaluation by experts who could better recognize human creative agency in AI-assisted work. Our findings reveal a policy tension wherein simple AI-use labels can inadvertently weaken the human agency that transparency rules seek to protect. Regulators, platforms, and organizations should, therefore, complement disclosure requirements with audience AI literacy and more informative, process-based disclosures that show how people contributed through prompting, selection, revision, and editing.

Title: A Representative Sampling Method for Peer Encouragement Designs in Network Experiments
Authors: Yanyan Li, Sha Yang, Qing Liu
Affiliations: Department of Marketing & Entrepreneurship, C. T. Bauer College of Business, University of Houston, Houston, Texas 77004; Department of Marketing, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90007; and Department of Marketing, School of Business, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Department of Marketing, Wisconsin School of Business, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53706
Abstract: This paper proposes a representative ego network sampling method that controls sample contamination while preserving population representativeness for peer encouragement experiments.

Title: Choice Models and Permutation Invariance: Deep Demand Estimation in Differentiated Products Markets
Authors: Amandeep Singh, Ye Liu, Hema Yoganarasimhan
Affiliations: University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30308
Abstract: This paper proposes a fundamental characterization of choice functions for flexible, data-driven demand estimation in differentiated products markets, accommodating endogenous product features and enabling valid inference on economic objects such as price elasticities

Title: Explaining Corporate Tax Avoidance
Authors: Andrew Belnap, Kaitlyn Kroeger, Jacob Thornock
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; The University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa 52242; Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah 84602
Abstract: The tax avoidance literature identifies dozens of variables that are related to corporate tax avoidance, but it lacks a framework for understanding the relative importance of these variables and the theories that drive these relations. We distill decades of tax avoidance research into key theories and create a unified sample that contains 31 independent variables from prior literature to quantify the relative and total importance of proposed explanations. Using Shapley value variance decomposition, we show that investment-related factors and operating metrics dominate effective tax rate (ETR) measures and consistently rank high across a range of tax avoidance proxies. When we examine the relative importance of time-invariant effects, we find that manager, firm, and segment fixed effects explain the greatest variation in tax avoidance. We offer several actionable opportunities for future research and offer several key takeaways for researchers and policymakers. This paper was accepted by Eric So, accounting. Title: Credit Ratings and Investments
Authors: Anna Bayona, Oana Peia, Razvan Vlahu
Affiliations: Esade Business School, Universitat Ramon Llull, 08034 Barcelona, Spain; School of Economics, University College Dublin, Belfield, Dublin 4, Ireland; Financial Stability Division, De Nederlandsche Bank, 1000 AB Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract: We study the impact of potentially inflated credit ratings in bond markets using experimental coordination games. Theoretical models featuring a feedback effect between capital markets and the real economy suggest that inflated ratings can have both positive and negative effects. Comparing markets with and without a credit rating agency, we find that ratings significantly influence investor behavior and capital allocation to firms. While we find evidence for both positive and negative real effects of potentially inflated ratings, the presence of a rating has an overall positive effect. We examine the mechanisms underlying these real effects and find that they operate mainly through investors’ beliefs about others’ behavior, and less so through beliefs about the firm’s fundamentals. Title: Risk Pricing Under Gain–Loss Asymmetry
Authors: Marianne Andries
Affiliations: University of Southern California, Centre for Economic Policy Research, Los Angeles, California 90089
Abstract: We propose a novel gain–loss asymmetric utility model—losses relative to a reference point incur discontinuously more disutility than comparable gains—under which we derive closed-form asset pricing solutions within the workhorse “long-run risk” asset pricing model. Our formal analysis reveals gain–loss asymmetry has a dual impact on risk prices. First, a level effect: the expected excess returns of risky assets are made higher and the risk-free rate lower by the kink in the preferences. Second, a cross-sectional effect: the increase in expected returns for an additional unit of risk is higher (lower) for safer (riskier) assets, so expected returns increase nonlinearly with risk exposures. This second effect, absent in standard smooth utility models, can help rationalize, both qualitatively and quantitatively, key puzzles in empirical finance—the fit of the security market line and the downward-sloping term structure of equity risk premia—without compromising on the model’s ability to match the equity premium in the data. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02286 .

Title: Enhancing the Benefits of Dual Sourcing with Upstream Visibility
Authors: Pavithra Harsha, Ashish Jagmohan, Retsef Levi, Elisabeth Paulson, Georgia Perakis
Affiliations: IBM Thomas J Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, New York 10598; Emergence AI, New York, New York 10018; Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142; Technology and Operations Management Unit, Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts 02163
Abstract: Problem definition: Yield uncertainty is a ubiquitous and serious issue in supply chain management. A common mitigation strategy for buyers is dual sourcing: ordering the same good from multiple suppliers to hedge against uncertainty in the suppliers’ ability to fulfill orders. In the literature, it is typically assumed that there is a single buyer that knows or can learn the reliability of each supplier, which is assumed to be exogenous to the buyer’s ordering behavior. However, in supply chains with a large number of buyers, this assumption is limiting. Methodology/results: We study a stylized supply chain model consisting of n buyers and two suppliers. The buyers do not observe their suppliers’ reliabilities a priori but can learn about them over time based on their interactions with the suppliers (in the learning setting) or through supply chain visibility (in the upstream visibility setting). We allow for the suppliers’ reliabilities to be impacted by the buyers’ ordering behaviors; when suppliers receive larger order volumes, it diminishes their ability to meet a buyer’s order in full, and thus, their perceived reliability falls. As a result, buyers—who cannot distinguish whether shortfalls are caused by low supplier capacity versus order congestion—may increase order quantities to hedge against shortage risk. We study the long-run ordering dynamics that emerge from this model in both settings. Managerial implications: We find that without visibility, “overordering spirals” can emerge, whereby buyers continue to inflate orders to the suppliers because they perceive shortages. This phenomenon has been observed when sudden, unexplained shortages occur, such as in the semiconductor or drug manufacturing industries. Interestingly, this can occur even in cases where shortages would not arise under truthful ordering but are created by inflated orders. Upstream visibility can be used as a tool to combat these spirals and can benefit both the buyers and the suppliers. Title: A Sample-Based Approach to the Price-Setting Newsvendor Problem with Limited Demand Information
Authors: Rongchuan He, Ye Lu
Affiliations: International Institute of Finance, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui 230000, China; Department of Operations and Decision Analytics, College of Business, City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon, Hong Kong
Abstract: Problem definition: We consider a price-setting newsvendor problem in which the demand distribution is unknown. We assume that the retailer exercises only a few price points with a sample set of demand realizations for each exercised price. Given this limited demand information, we define an ambiguity set and study two robust optimization models that maximize the worst-case profit (maxmin profit) and minimize the maximum regret (minmax regret), respectively. Methodology/results: These two robust models are reduced to easy-to-solve optimization problems. Compared with the maximal profit under complete demand information, we find that with only a few price points, we can achieve more than 90% of the maximal profit on average and around 70% of the maximal profit in the worst case. Our method is purely data driven and model free; that is, we do not assume that the demand model follows any specific form. This approach has the advantage of avoiding model mismatches in practice. Managerial implications: We show that this new method outperforms traditional methods, such as regressions, and other model-specific methods. We also propose demand learning methods with guaranteed convergence rates when the number of exercised prices increases. Funding: R. Title: Mixing Motives: Political Donations by Corporate Executives
Authors: Benjamin Barber, Daniel J. Blake
Affiliations: IE Business School, IE University, 28046 Madrid, Spain
Abstract: What motivates corporate executives to make political donations? Scholars interested in political ideology generally assign expressive motivations to executive donations, whereas corporate political activity scholars view executives as largely strategic donors. This study reconciles these two contrasting perspectives by reconceptualizing executives as mixed-motive donors who allocate their donations both strategically and expressively. To support this position, we construct the most comprehensive data set to date on executive donations from 1980 to 2024 and develop a measure of mixed-motive donations that reflects both expressive and strategic giving. Using nonexecutive donors as a counterfactual baseline of expressive donors, we provide evidence that bipartisan donations and donations to politically influential members of Congress are examples of strategic giving. We find that executives devote a larger share of their donations to strategic giving driven by their role as executives. This supports the argument, rooted in resource dependence theory, that executives face professional incentives to donate strategically. However, we also find evidence that a nontrivial portion of executives’ donations are expressive and that strategic giving varies across individuals and time. We find that variance in mixed-motive giving can be explained partly by executives’ compensation elasticity, firm size, political risk exposure, and whether an executive is the CEO of the company. Overall, our analysis reveals that scholars should refrain from making uniform assumptions about executives’ motivations to donate and view them as a varied group of mixed-motive donors. Title: Ecosystem Orchestration: Mechanisms, Regimes, and Theories of the Firm Foundations
Authors: Sergei Mozheiko, Xianwei Shi, Tony W. Tong
Affiliations: Hang Seng University of Hong Kong; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; University of Colorado Boulder
Abstract: Value creation is increasingly shifting from standalone firms in linear value chains toward multilaterally coordinated efforts among heterogeneous actors in ecosystems. Yet, we know relatively little about how coordination unfolds when value creation activities are distributed in this manner. As a focal entity grows increasingly reliant on actors beyond its formal authority, value creation and capture depend on aligning and steering these interdependent actors through indirect means—an approach best described as “orchestration.” We define “ecosystem orchestration” as the application of control and coordination mechanisms beyond organizational boundaries to integrate complementary efforts across ecosystem participants. First, through a comprehensive integrative review, we identify four categories of mechanisms: codified, cognitive, incentive, and hierarchical. We then examine how these mechanisms are bundled into distinct orchestration regimes across platform, industrial, innovation, and entrepreneurial ecosystems. Further, we highlight salient connections between these mechanisms and classic theories of the firm—resource-based view, property rights theory, transaction cost economics, and knowledge-based view. By moving beyond generic notions of orchestration and revealing its underlying mechanisms, we establish a clearer foundation for advancing ecosystem research, integrate the fragmented ecosystem orchestration literature, and anchor it more firmly in established theories. Finally, we conclude by outlining conceptual, empirical, and methodological directions for future inquiry.

Title: The Rising Tide Lifts Some Interest Rates: Climate Change, Natural Disasters, and Loan Pricing
Authors: Ricardo Correa, Ai He, Christoph Herpfer, Ugur Lel
Abstract: ABSTRACT Banks adjust loan spreads after observing natural disasters linked to climate change. We isolate this updating process by identifying loans to borrowers at risk of, but not directly affected by, such disasters. Loan spreads for these borrowers spike in both primary and secondary markets, while no such updating occurs for non–climate‐related disasters. Evidence suggests a heightened perceived credit risk, which nonetheless cannot fully explain the increase in rates. Taken altogether, increased spreads are explained primarily by salience bias, as they are short‐lived and amplified by media attention. This salience impacts financial decisions at bank‐dependent firms.

Title: Dynamic Self‐Fulfilling Fire Sales
Authors: Paymon Khorrami, Fernando Mendo
Abstract: ABSTRACT Why do fire sales occur if many risks are hedgeable? We study a version of Brunnermeier and Sannikov (2014, American Economic Review 104, 379–421) in which all fundamental risks can be hedged frictionlessly. Our analysis shows that fire sales are inherently self‐fulfilling. Fundamental shocks can never cause fire sales, and an efficient, safe equilibrium exists. On the other hand, there exists an equilibrium in which agents coordinate fire sales on nonfundamental shocks. A simple refinement based on vanishingly small perceived fundamental risk eliminates the safe equilibrium and selects the fire‐sale equilibrium as the unique outcome.

Title: Am I Just a Digital Puppet? Exploring the Impact of Electronic Performance Monitoring and Supervisor Monitoring on Employee Performance From the Perspective of Objectification Theory
Authors: Lixun Zheng, Wen Cheng, Wenzhu Lu, Xiaoming Zheng
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China; School of Business Guangdong University of Foreign Studies Guangzhou China; School of Management Lanzhou University Lanzhou China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Electronic performance monitoring (EPM) has been widely used in organizations in the expectation of promoting performance. However, its effectiveness sometimes falls short of these expectations. Most previous studies have examined EPM's side effects from the perspective of psychological reactance, treating it simply as a monitoring stressor. To extend this literature, we draw on workplace objectification theory and propose that EPM fosters employees' perceived objectification by signaling objectifying cues, which in turn undermines employee job performance. Moreover, supervisor monitoring styles (observational and interactional) can either strengthen or weaken the relationship between EPM and perceived objectification. We tested our model using an online experiment with 199 US participants and a multi‐wave field survey with 294 Chinese employees, and all hypotheses were supported. Theoretically, this research complements the psychological reactance perspective in EPM research by introducing perceived objectification as a humanity‐related mechanism through which EPM may shape employee performance. We also advance workplace objectification theory by extending its scope from human–human interactions to human–technology interactions. Practically, we offer guidance on preserving employees' humanity while adopting technological and human monitoring to maintain performance.

Title: The Falling Roe and Relocation of Skilled Women
Authors: Yupeng Lin, Michael Shen, Rui Shi, Jean (Jieyin) Zeng
Affiliations: National University of Singapore Singapore Singapore; City University of Hong Kong Kowloon Tong Hong Kong; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Shanghai China
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the impact of abortion restrictions on the geographic mobility of college‐educated skilled women. Exploiting the staggered adoption of Targeted Regulation of Abortion Providers (TRAP) laws across US states that restrict women's access to abortion, we find that skilled women who relocate exhibit a greater propensity to move to states without TRAP laws (non‐TRAP states) than they did prior to the TRAP law adoption. This pattern is stronger among women in more liberal and less religious areas than among women in more conservative and more religious areas. These findings are consistent with the view that relocation decisions are often driven by the alignment between personal values and the local policy environment. We use the audit industry as a specific setting to address the implications for employer performance. We find that TRAP law adoption increases female auditor turnover at local offices relative to same‐firm offices in non‐TRAP states, and the resulting loss of human capital lowers audit quality.

Title: Warner Bros. Discovery: Seeking Growth With Generative AI
Authors: George Westerman, David Kiron
Abstract: Warner Bros. Discovery advanced its AI strategy by putting creators first and treating AI as a growth opportunity, not a cost-cutting tool. This case study shows how trust, governance, and business ownership are critical to scaling AI innovation.

Title: Virtual influencer marketing: A meta-analytic review
Authors: Mojtaba Moji Barari, Martin Eisend, Alicia Kulczynski
Abstract: Abstract Virtual influencers have become an established part of influencer marketing, yet their effectiveness, the mechanisms underlying their persuasive impact, and the boundary conditions shaping these effects remain unclear. We address these questions through a meta-analysis of 210 independent experimental studies and 643 effect sizes. Virtual influencers generate greater novelty but lower credibility than human influencers, revealing a systematic trade-off between novelty- and credibility-based persuasion, with the relative importance of these mechanisms shifting over time from novelty toward credibility. Virtual influencer effectiveness further depends on anthropomorphic design and contextual congruence. Highly anthropomorphic virtual influencers benefit from artificial intelligence integration, futuristic positioning, and rational, proximal messaging, whereas low-anthropomorphism virtual influencers perform better with emotional and distal framing. Meta-analytic structural equation modeling supports a dual-pathway process in which credibility-based indirect effects are stronger for highly anthropomorphic virtual influencers, whereas novelty-based indirect effects are stronger for low-anthropomorphism virtual influencers. These results establish anthropomorphism as a structural boundary condition in influencer marketing.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Collaborative vehicle routing with strategic request acceptance: The impact of profit sharing
Authors: Yannick Oskar Scherr, Margaretha Gansterer, Richard F. Hartl
Abstract: We investigate the operational problem of carriers receiving pickup-and-delivery requests that must be answered immediately and fulfilled the next day with a given fleet. Before fulfillment, carriers participate in a collaboration to exchange requests with other carriers in a combinatorial auction. Submitted requests are grouped into bundles that are redistributed according to carriers’ bids to minimize costs. Total auction profits are shared among carriers using a profit-sharing mechanism. We model each carrier's sequential optimization problem and use heuristic routing approaches. For making dynamic acceptance decisions, we propose a two-step policy considering strategic rejection, i.e., rejecting also requests that could be fulfilled with currently available capacities. The first step decides on accepting and fulfilling a request, while the second step decides on overbooking a request and submitting it to the auction. After modeling the carriers’ decision-making process, we investigate the impact of the exchange mechanism, particularly the profit-sharing mechanism, on carriers’ behavior. We propose a Shapley-Value based profit-sharing mechanism and a new adjustable mechanism in which the degree to which carriers receive equal auction outcomes can be adjusted. Experiments on homogeneous settings (carriers use the same strategy) show revenue gains (up to 15.19%) and cost savings (up to 10.43%) compared to benchmarks. Heterogeneous settings (different strategies) provide insights into incentives to deviate from the best strategies based on the profit-sharing mechanism. Our results suggest that intermediate settings of the adjustable mechanism are particularly effective in counteracting deviations. Thus, mechanism design impacts both the success of the collaboration and carriers’ customer acceptance.

Title: An extension of Hu’s algorithm for resource leveling and some related results
Authors: Péter Györgyi, Tamás Kis
Abstract: In this paper we consider resource leveling problems with precedence constraints in which jobs requiring a common resource have to be scheduled in order to minimize a convex function of the resource usage over time. We consider two variants of this problem. In the first one, all the jobs have unit processing time, a common deadline and require one unit from the common resource. Moreover, the precedence constraints induce a set of disjoint in-trees on the job set. We propose a polynomial time algorithm which solves the resource leveling problem for arbitrary convex functions. Our method builds on some of the ideas of Hu's algorithm for solving the makespan minimization problem in a parallel machine environment with unit-time jobs and with precedence constraints inducing an in-tree. In the second variant, we have a parallel machine environment and unit-time jobs connected by arbitrary precedence constraints. Since deciding if a feasible schedule of a given makespan exists is NP-hard, our goal is to transform any feasible schedule by at most doubling its makespan while approximating the best possible resource usage cost among all schedules with a makespan bounded by that of the original schedule.

Title: When is Separate Sales Optimal?
Authors: Changhyun Kwak
Affiliations: Institute of Economics, Academia Sinica
Abstract: Abstract This paper studies a multi-product monopolist facing a privately informed consumer with additive and type-increasing valuations. Separate monopoly pricing is robustly optimal with respect to the type distribution if and only if the marginal rate of substitution between each pair of goods is monotone. This result is obtained by extending the conventional Myersonian approach.

Title: Code and Data Repository for Decision-Driven Regularization: A Blended Model for Learning and Optimization
Authors: Gar Goei Loke, Qinshen Tang, Yangge Xiao, Xun Zhang
Abstract: The code and data in this repository are used in the research reported in the paper Decision-Driven Regularization: A Blended Model for Learning and Optimization by Gar Goei Loke, Qinshen Tang, Yangge Xiao, and Xun Zhang.

Title: Beliefs about the relationship between work and personal life: development and validation of three work-life belief scales
Authors: Sabrina L. Speights, Lisa M. Leslie, Eden B. King, Elinor Flynn, Judith A. Clair
Abstract: Theory suggests work-life outcomes are shaped by three beliefs regarding how work and personal life relate to each other: fixed-expandable-pie beliefs (whether work and life compete with versus enhance one another), segmentation-integration beliefs (whether work and life operate as separate versus related domains), and work-life priority beliefs (whether work versus personal life takes precedence over the other domain). Yet no measure of work-life beliefs exists, which is an impediment to understanding their ability to advance the work-life literature. In 15 studies ( N = 6,568), using samples drawn from different populations (adults and students in the United States, adults with diverse cultural backgrounds in the United Kingdom, adults in Ghana, adults in South Korea), we develop measures of three work-life beliefs and document their utility for understanding the work-life interface. We find that work-life beliefs can be conceptualized as three or six dimensions, and that the measures have a replicable factor structure, are reliable, and have discriminant validity, in that they are distinct from other work-life constructs and beliefs about hard work and leisure. The work-life belief measures also have criterion validity; they contribute to understanding of work-life experiences and behaviors, both indirectly and directly. Our research advances the literature by providing insight into the nature of work-life beliefs and demonstrating their relevance for understanding the work-life interface. By developing measures, we also provide tools that can be used in future work to develop, test, and refine theory regarding the implications of work-life beliefs for understanding any number of additional phenomena.
Journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

Title: How experience moderates the impact of AI suggestions on researchers' perceptions of their ideas
Authors: Matthias Tröbinger, Anil R. Doshi, Sen Chai
Abstract: At the heart of scientific discovery are researchers who identify ideas worthy of inquiry. In performing research tasks, researchers increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. While this technology offers the promise of increased efficiency across the research process, little is known about how generative AI assists researchers with the generation of initial research ideas—one of the most fundamental tasks in science—and their willingness to adopt it for such purpose. In a pre-registered randomized online experiment with 310 researchers and a follow-up ideation study with 28 researchers, we show how one's research experience plays a role in receiving generative AI suggestions when formulating new research ideas. Experience negatively moderates both the incorporation of generative AI suggestions as well as its effect on perceived novelty and impact of the researcher's idea. We also find that generative AI may be reshaping research ideation by adding a layer of non-human exchange that precedes feedback from human experts. By focusing on the critical moment at which research ideas spark, we provide an initial understanding of how researchers respond to generative AI at a time when the paradigm of human knowledge production may be shifting from a human-only to a joint human-AI model.

Title: Birds of a feather: How influencer-brand fit drives product sales in livestream commerce
Authors: Shaoling Katee Zhang, Yao Shi, Huigang Liang, Yajiong Lucky Xue
Abstract: Influencer-brand fit is central to influencer selection, yet its impact on immediate sales in livestream commerce remains unclear. This research introduces follower-based fit (i.e., the similarity between an influencer’s followers and a brand’s target consumers) as a distinct dimension alongside the widely studied image-based fit (i.e., the alignment between an influencer’s persona and a brand’s image). Using two large-scale observational datasets, we show that follower-based fit is the dominant driver of immediate sales in livestream commerce. However, its effect is attenuated when image-based fit is high. Two experiments reveal the underlying mechanisms: the sales effect of follower-based fit is fully mediated by self-brand congruence, but this effect is impaired by high image-based fit, which shifts followers’ attribution of the influencer’s agency role from follower-serving (i.e., serve the followers’ interests) to brand-serving (i.e., serve the brand’s interests). Additional observational evidence indicates that this backfire effect does not arise in new influencer-brand partnerships but emerges and persists once partnerships become established. Our findings extend influencer‑brand fit literature and provide guidance for optimizing influencer selection strategies in livestream commerce.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Earnings management in private equity portfolio firms during fundraising
Authors: Brian K. Baik
Abstract: I study whether private equity (PE) investors’ fundraising periods are associated with increased earnings management (EM) among portfolio firms. Using a novel matched sample of European buyout funds and private firm financials, I find that EM intensifies during fundraising periods among portfolio firms backed by a predictable subset of PE investors. Specifically, I find the effects appear mostly in portfolio firms backed by low reputation PE investors rather than across the entire sample. These effects are economically meaningful, consistent with qualitative evidence from interviews with PE professionals. Cross-sectional analyses show that EM increases when investors have stronger incentives and greater ability to influence reporting and where institutional guardrails are weaker. I also document that certain forms of EM are associated with longer future portfolio firm holding periods and worse exit outcomes. Together, the results reveal how investor reputation and fundraising incentives can shape private firm reporting in opaque markets.

Title: Insider trading after the 2022 Rule 10b5-1 amendment
Authors: Sehwa Kim, Seil Kim, Shiva Rajgopal
Abstract: We investigate the impact of the controversial 2022 amendment to Rule 10b5-1, which imposed a cooling-off period and restricted overlapping and single-trade plans on prearranged insider transactions. Our evidence is consistent with the amendment leading insiders to (i) execute stock sales under 10b5-1 plans with longer cooling-off periods; (ii) curtail opportunistic sales under 10b5-1 plans prior to stock price drops or earnings misses; (iii) limit the backdating of stock gifts; and (iv) decrease the granting of options around material information events. Further evidence suggests a reduction in opportunistic 10b5-1 trades rather than a migration toward non-10b5-1 sales. We find mixed evidence on the amendment's effect on price efficiency. Finally, terminations of 10b5-1 plans are associated with positive subsequent stock returns, suggesting that insiders avoid selling when they expect favorable news. Overall, our findings indicate that the amendment substantially curtailed the opportunistic use of 10b5-1 plans, its primary objective.

Title: Joint weak disposability in benefit-of-the-doubt models: methodology and structural analysis of country performance
Authors: Hirofumi Fukuyama, Yong Tan, Peter Wanke
Abstract: We extend the conventional Benefit-of-the-Doubt (BoD) approach by explicitly incorporating undesirable sub-indicators—variables typically excluded from standard models or treated under the unrealistic assumption that they can be reduced independently of desirable sub-indicators. Our method introduces the principle of joint weak disposability for both desirable (“good”) and undesirable (“bad”) outputs within the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) framework, ensuring a consistent treatment of substitutability between them. By interpreting DEA outputs as sub-indicators in BoD, the framework acknowledges that bad sub-indicators cannot be reduced independently, nor offset by increases in good sub-indicators, reflecting the structural and economic constraints countries face in managing burdens. To demonstrate its value, we apply the model to a global panel of countries from 2013 to 2021 and conduct a second-stage analysis of the drivers of cross-country performance differences. The findings highlight three main insights: (i) burden-to-benefit ratios exert a strong negative effect on performance, (ii) returns-to-burden conditions play a significant moderating role, and (iii) systematic disparities persist across income groups. Taken together, the proposed framework delivers both methodological innovation and practical guidance for macro-level performance assessment, offering a more realistic and policy-relevant evaluation of national outcomes.

Title: Correction to: A Further Augmentation of the Solow Model and the Empirics of Economic Growth for OECD Countries
Dollar Asset Holdings and Hedging around the Globe
Authors: Wenxin Du, Amy W Huber
Affiliations: Harvard Business School and NBER; The Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: Abstract We collect and analyze detailed filings from global institutional investors to estimate foreign investors’ U.S. dollar (USD) security holdings and currency hedging. Over two decades, foreign USD holdings grew sixfold, while hedge ratios rose by 15 percentage points after the 2008–2009 crisis. Currency hedging across mutual funds, pensions, and insurance reached $2 trillion by 2019. Hedging demand varies across investors, currency areas, and banking systems. We show that expected FX returns, beyond variance minimization, drive currency exposure in portfolios. Finally, we demonstrate and quantify how aggregate hedging demand affects hedging costs in the presence of constrained intermediaries.

Title: Pension Liquidity Risk
Authors: Kristy A E Jansen, Sven Klingler, Angelo Ranaldo, Patty Duijm
Affiliations: Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California, CEPR, and De Nederlandsche Bank , USA and Netherlands; Frankfurt School of Finance and Management; University of Basel and Swiss Finance Institute; De Nederlandsche Bank
Abstract: Abstract Pension funds use interest rate swaps to hedge the interest rate risk arising from their liabilities. Analyzing regulatory data on Dutch pension funds, we show that pension funds with worse funding ratios, indicating greater fragility, use swaps more aggressively. These swap positions expose pension funds to the risk of margin calls, which can exceed 6% of their total assets, when interest rates rise. Pension funds respond to realized margin calls by selling safe government bonds with medium-term maturities. This procyclical selling behavior adversely affects the prices of the sold bonds and thereby exposes pension funds to market liquidity risk.

Title: The Impact of Strategic Leaders’ International Experience on Organizations: An Integrative Review and Multilevel Framework
Authors: Fei Qin, Klaus E. Meyer, Sabina Tasheva Nielsen
Affiliations: University of Bath; Ivey Business School; University of Sydney; Copenhagen Business School
Abstract: Internationally experienced business leaders bring distinct human capital, social capital, and cognitive schemas into organizations, influence strategic orientation through their decision-making, and in turn shape organizations’ strategies and performance. The impact of the international experience (IE) of an organization’s upper echelon has been studied in various bodies of management literature, varying in terms of the theoretical perspectives, conceptualizations of the IE construct, and outcomes considered. However, the effects are not straightforward with regard to which elements of IE affect which aspects of organizational dynamics, and how. This review integrates separate streams of organizational research to develop a more holistic understanding of the role of the IE held by strategic leaders such as chief executive officers, entrepreneurial founders, top management teams, and boards of directors, and its impact on organizational strategies and performance. We refine the conceptualization of the IE construct at multiple levels of analysis and explore cross-level mechanisms suggested by multiple theories to develop an integrative framework that links strategic leaders’ IE to organizational decisions, strategies, and performance. On this basis, we propose an agenda for future research.

Title: Predictive Production-and-Service Planning: Ambiguity Aversion with Performance Guarantees
Authors: Yuchen Mao, Francisco Saldanha-da-Gama, Shuming Wang, Shouyang Wang
Affiliations: School of Economics & Management, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China; and Department of Statistics, Rutgers University, Piscataway, New Jersey 08854; Sheffield University Management School, The University of Sheffield, Sheffield S10 1FL, United Kingdom; Academy of Mathematics & Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China; and School of Entrepreneurship and Management, ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai 201210, China
Abstract: We consider a two-stage joint production and service planning problem under demand ambiguity. The product-service provider receives a fixed amount of revenue from the recipient in advance (first-stage), and is committed to fulfill all the demands realized over a specific period (second-stage). The provider aims to determine the portfolio of products with the associated service levels and the capacity to maximize the expected total profit. We study the problem in a data-driven setting assuming the historical information on demand and the associated covariates are available, where the service decision is itself a key covariate for demand. In order to capture the effect of demand correlation and variance-heterogeneity across products and the effect of service dependency under demand ambiguity, we construct a predictive ambiguity set leveraging seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) estimated with feasible generalized least squares (FGLS), which treats the service level as a regressor and addresses the heteroskedasticity. We then develop a decision-dependent two-stage distributionally robust optimization (DRO) model. Operationally, we identify that the developed predictive DRO model can be reformulated as an empirical counterpart under the predicted demand distribution regularized by a perceived shortage cost as the shadow price for ambiguity aversion. Exploiting this structure, we analyze the ambiguity-averse operational properties and risk exposure in terms of worst-case performance sensitivity. Statistically, our approach enjoys finite-sample performance guarantee and asymptotic consistency under several regularity conditions. Computationally, the proposed model can be reformulated as a mixed-integer conic program that enjoys an appealing structure for optimization. Finally, sufficient numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. This paper was accepted by J. George Shanthikumar, data science. Funding: S. M. F. Saldanha-da-Gama and S. M. Wang are also jointly supported by the President’s International Fellowship Initiative [Grant 2025PVA0080] of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). S. Y.
